paragraphs.source_en: The function of ceramic pots as containers for storing food is also possible (Barich 1998a; Rice 1999). Pottery would have been mostly reserved for precious food or resources, such as fish oil or particular vegetables of fruits, whereas more common supplies would be stored in containers of other materials.

paragraphs.source_en: Although the purely practical function of the earliest pottery cannot be excluded, evidence suggests that it was adopted initially as a prestige technology. According to Barich (1998b) the scarcity of fragments in the earliest settlements of the 10th millennium BP indicates that vessels were precious and they had not been destined for domestic use, but rather had been reserved for particular purposes. Barich (1998b) concludes that at that time, pottery must have had more of a symbolic meaning than an economic role and its growth occurred from 8,500 BP at the same time as the intensification of wild cereal collection in the Mesolithic period.

paragraphs.source_en: The symbolic function related to ritual and/or to status was also postulated by Rice (1999) for the earliest pottery throughout the world. Ceramic pots were special-purpose vessels which would have played an important role in feasting occasions, primarily as vessels for holding and serving the ritual food. For this reason the containers should be considered both as wealth because they represent a prestigious new technology, and intrinsic components of social relations. According to Rice (1999) the decoration of food containers may indicate socioeconomic uses and may be a function of their role in distribution and exchange among groups. These decorated vessels could have been prestigious vehicles for displaying and communicating messages of social identity, and could have been objects of trade.
